title: Discriminated unions: the single most important pattern
summary: Give every variant of a union a shared literal tag field. The compiler then narrows the variant from the tag alone, and a switch over the tag can be checked for exhaustiveness with never.

examples.title: A run result as a discriminated union

annotations.note: status is a literal type "ok", not string. That literal is the discriminator: comparing it anywhere narrows the whole object type.
The failed variant carries an error and no rows. Impossible states like "ok with error message" or "failed with rows" are unrepresentable.
Narrowing happens on the tag alone — no type assertions, no casts. Inside case "failed", TypeScript knows error exists and rows doesn't.
The never default is a compile-time exhaustiveness check: add a variant without extending this switch and tsc refuses to build.

use_cases: API responses (ok/failed), state machines (idle/loading/ready/error), UI events
Anywhere you would otherwise have optional fields that are only sometimes present
strengths: Unlike optional-field soup (rows?: T[]; error?: string), variants document which fields belong together
switch + never catches every unhandled variant at compile time, for free
Narrowing works through any check on the tag: switch, if, ternary, destructuring
weaknesses: Requires discipline at the boundaries: network JSON needs runtime validation (zod) before you can trust the tag
Deep unions of unions can get noisy; keep variants flat where you can

pitfalls.title: Typing the tag as string instead of a literal
pitfalls.detail: status: string narrows nothing. The tag must be a literal type ('ok' | 'failed').

pitfalls.title: Optional fields instead of variants
pitfalls.detail: rows?: T[] invites checking nothing. With variants, using rows in the failed branch is a compile error.

pitfalls.title: Assertions (as) instead of narrowing
pitfalls.detail: res as FailedResult silences the compiler and lies at runtime. Narrow from the tag; assert only when you truly know more than tsc.

options: A literal-typed shared field identifies each variant
quiz.why: The literal tag is what lets control-flow analysis narrow the variant everywhere it's compared.

quiz.q: Adding a 'cancelled' variant without touching the switch — when does it break?
options: At compile time, via the never check
quiz.why: The default branch assigns the variant to never, which no type except never satisfies, so tsc errors.

body:
## Concept

A discriminated union is a union of object types that share one field — the *tag* — whose
type is a string (or number) literal unique to each variant. Checking the tag narrows the
object type: `if (r.status === "failed")` gives you the failed variant, with its fields and
nothing else.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: a tagged union (`struct { enum tag; union {…} }`) done by the type system, with the
  forgetting-to-check-the-tag bug made impossible.
- Java/Python: sealed interfaces / subclasses and instanceof; discriminated unions are the
  data-only, serialization-friendly version.
- JS: you've written this shape as plain objects with a `type` field (Redux actions). The
  difference is TypeScript checking the tag and the exhaustiveness.

## Design notes

Model a value as *exactly one variant* and make illegal states unrepresentable: a request
either has rows or an error, never both, never neither. Combined with a `never`-checked
switch, the compiler forces every consumer to grow when the union grows — this is the
frontend's equivalent of Go's "accept interfaces, return structs": a default shape for
everything that crosses feature boundaries.
